content: Inhalation of carbon particles in large quantities can be hazardous, as it may irritate lung tissues and lead to the development of coal worker's pneumoconiosis, a form of congestive lung disease. Similarly, diamond dust, often used as an abrasive, can cause harm if it is inhaled or ingested. Microparticles of carbon, which are generated in diesel engine exhaust fumes, can accumulate in the lungs over time. The harmful effects in such cases may not necessarily arise from the carbon itself but rather from contaminants associated with the carbon particles, such as organic chemicals or heavy metals. Carbon is also highly combustible and can burn vigorously and brightly in the presence of air at elevated temperatures. An example of this is the Windscale fire, which occurred due to the sudden release of stored Wigner energy in the graphite core of a nuclear reactor. Large deposits of coal, which have remained chemically inert for hundreds of millions of years in the absence of oxygen, can spontaneously ignite when exposed to air. This phenomenon is often observed in coal mine waste tips. Carbon compounds exhibit a wide range of properties, encompassing both lethal toxins and essential biomolecules. Examples of toxic carbon compounds include tetrodotoxin, the lectin ricin derived from the seeds of the castor oil plant Ricinus communis, cyanide (CN⁻), and carbon monoxide. On the other hand, carbon-based compounds such as glucose and proteins are indispensable for sustaining life.
